reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: The high-pitched, monotone, cat-like cry in infancy gives the syndrome its name and reflects abnormal laryngeal and neurological development; it often diminishes with age
Caused by a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, with phenotype severity broadly correlating with deletion size and specific critical regions
Facial features include microcephaly, a rounded face, hypertelorism, epicanthic folds, down-slanting palpebral fissures and low-set ears, with the face lengthening over time
Prenatal-onset growth restriction, marked feeding difficulty and hypotonia are common in infancy
Most deletions are de novo, but a minority arise from an unbalanced parental translocation, so parental karyotyping is essential for recurrence-risk counselling
Severe intellectual disability with markedly limited expressive language is typical, though receptive skills are relatively better
Behavioural features can include hyperactivity, self-injury and stereotypies
reference.pathophysiology: Cri-du-chat syndrome arises from a terminal or interstitial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p), producing haploinsufficiency for genes in this region. Loss of specific critical intervals correlates with the characteristic cry and with the degree of intellectual disability, and candidate genes such as those influencing telomerase regulation and neuronal cytoskeletal proteins have been implicated. The reduced dosage of these developmentally important genes disrupts laryngeal, craniofacial and central nervous system formation. Deletions are commonly de novo and paternal in origin, but can result from malsegregation of a balanced parental rearrangement.
additionalDifferentials: Prader-Willi syndrome in the hypotonic neonate
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray to define the deletion and its size
Karyotype to detect an underlying translocation, with parental karyotypes for recurrence risk
FISH targeting the 5p critical region where confirmation is needed
Feeding and swallowing assessment in infancy
Hearing and vision testing to support developmental progress
redFlags: Failure to thrive from severe feeding difficulty and recurrent aspiration
Unrecognised congenital heart disease causing cardiorespiratory compromise
Stridor or airway obstruction related to laryngeal abnormality
Self-injurious behaviour requiring safeguarding and specialist input
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have severe intellectual disability but can achieve some self-care and communication skills with early intervention; survival into adulthood is usual. Outcome depends largely on associated malformations, especially cardiac and respiratory, and on deletion size.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal standard karyotype excludes the diagnosis when small deletions require microarray or FISH
Omitting parental karyotyping and mis-stating recurrence risk when a translocation is present
Attributing feeding failure to behaviour rather than oromotor dysfunction
Underestimating relatively preserved receptive language and social ability
